fr:title.text: A Pallas kernel is an opaque custom call

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A Pallas kernel is an opaque custom call

fr:mainmatter.html:p: How does a Pallas or Triton kernel appear in a StableHLO dump?

html:div.html:details:
Answer As an opaque custom call (XLA custom call):
stablehlo.custom_call @tpu_custom_call(%a, %b) {backend_config = "...", api_version = 2 : i32} : (tensor<8x128xf32>, ...) -> tensor<8x128xf32>
On GPU the target is @triton_kernel_call instead.
The kernel body is not in this IR. It is serialised inside backend_config — a Mosaic module, or Triton IR (The prefix says which side of layout assignment) — and XLA treats the whole thing as a black box with declared operands, results, and effects.
That is the trade you accept when you write a kernel by hand: you get control of the inner loop, and you give up every cross-op optimisation at the boundary, because the compiler cannot fuse across something it cannot see (A custom call is a black box XLA cannot fuse across).

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: References
Context
StableHLO

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The MLIR dialect JAX lowers to and XLA ingests — the versioned, portable contract between frameworks and compilers (Lifecycle of a JAX program). Print it with jax.jit(f).lower(x).as_text() (Three calls, three IR levels).

The word doing the work in the name is stable. It is one of three HLO-family dialects and the only one with compatibility guarantees: chlo above it is sugar that gets decomposed, mhlo below it is XLA's unstable internal dialect (chlo desugars, stablehlo is stable, mhlo is internal). A serialised StableHLO program is expected to keep deserialising across compiler versions, which is what makes it a sensible artifact to ship, cache, or hand to a different backend.

Read it to answer one specific question: what did JAX actually ask for? It sits at the boundary where a JAX bug becomes an XLA bug. Above it the shapes are still recognisably yours; below it, in optimized HLO, fusion and layout assignment have rewritten the program past easy comparison (Only after_optimizations matches the profile).

A hand-written kernel — Pallas or Triton — appears here as an opaque custom_call whose body is serialised into an attribute (A Pallas kernel is an opaque custom call), which is the first place you can see that XLA has been handed something it cannot look inside.

html:div.html:p: The same function one level down. tanh(x @ w + b), lowered with jax.jit(f).lower(x, w, b).as_text(). Compare it against the jaxpr of the same function:
Four things are worth noticing, and each is a card.

html:ul.html:li: It is ordinary MLIR: a builtin.module with attributes (Every dump is wrapped in a module), a func.func whose result carries an attribute JAX put there (Three attribute positions on a function), and pretty-printed ops (The pretty form is optional, the generic form always works).
The dot_general uses the sugar form contracting_dims = [1] x [0] rather than the #stablehlo.dot<> attribute (Batch, contract, free, and the output order is fixed) — same information, shorter.

The bias broadcast became two ops. dims = [1] maps the operand's single dimension to output dim 1, giving 1x4; a second broadcast_in_dim then stretches the size-1 dimension to 8 (broadcast_in_dim maps operand dims onto output dims). One jaxpr equation, two StableHLO ops.
No layouts anywhere. Those are assigned later, inside XLA (The layout is minor-to-major).

fr:title.text: chlo desugars, stablehlo is stable, mhlo is internal

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: chlo desugars, stablehlo is stable, mhlo is internal

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In a JAX/XLA dump, what are the chlo, stablehlo, and mhlo dialects, and how do they relate?

html:div.html:details:
Answer
chlo — "client" HLO: higher-level sugar that gets decomposed. Implicitly broadcasting binary ops, erf, top-k style helpers.
stablehlo — the stable, versioned, portable IR (StableHLO). This is what JAX emits and serialises today, and the compatibility boundary between frameworks and compilers.
mhlo — "meta" HLO: XLA's internal, unstable dialect, what stablehlo is converted into before XLA's own HLO proto (HLO).
The pipeline, in full (Lifecycle of a JAX program):
Python -> jaxpr -> chlo/stablehlo -> mhlo -> HLO -> optimized HLO -> backend (LLVM/PTX, Mosaic/LLO)
Only one of the three is a contract. stablehlo has version guarantees so a serialised program keeps deserialising; chlo and mhlo are implementation details you may read but must not depend on.

fr:title.text: broadcast_in_dim maps operand dims onto output dims

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: broadcast_in_dim maps operand dims onto output dims

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read %0 = stablehlo.broadcast_in_dim %a, dims = [1] : (tensor<3xf32>) -> tensor<2x3xf32>

html:div.html:details:
Answer dims maps each operand dimension to the output dimension it lands in. Here operand dim 0 (size 3) becomes output dim 1. Every output dimension not listed is a new broadcast dimension, and a listed dimension of size 1 may be stretched.
Two invariants make the attribute self-checking: the list length always equals the operand rank, and the values must be strictly increasing — so a broadcast can add and stretch dimensions but never permute them. A permutation needs a separate transpose (transpose dimensions read output from operand).
This is one of two dimension-list conventions and they read in opposite directions. Broadcast lists a target per operand dim; transpose lists a source per output dim. HLO's broadcast uses this same convention (broadcast dimensions read operand to output).

fr:title.text: Batch, contract, free, and the output order is fixed

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Batch, contract, free, and the output order is fixed

fr:mainmatter.html:p: How do you read a dot_general's dimension numbers? #stablehlo.dot<lhs_batching_dimensions = [0], rhs_batching_dimensions = [0], lhs_contracting_dimensions = [2], rhs_contracting_dimensions = [1]>

html:div.html:details:
Answer Every dimension is one of three kinds:
Batching — matched pairwise between lhs and rhs, and kept. These are independent problems solved side by side.
Contracting — matched pairwise and summed away. This is the reduction.
Free — everything else, and it survives into the output.
The output order is fixed, not chosen: batch dimensions, then lhs free dimensions in order, then rhs free dimensions in order. So the result shape is fully determined by the attribute and you never have to guess. Newer printers use the sugar contracting_dims = [2] x [1].
The same three-way split appears at every level — as dimension_numbers in a jaxpr (dimension_numbers is contracting then batch) and as lhs_batch_dims and friends in HLO (A dot's output order is batch, lhs free, rhs free) — which is what makes a matmul traceable straight down the stack.

fr:title.text: reduce takes a computation, not an enum

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: reduce takes a computation, not an enum

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Why does a stablehlo.reduce body look like a region? %r = stablehlo.reduce(%a init: %zero) applies stablehlo.add across dimensions = [1]

html:div.html:details:
Answer Because reduce takes a reducer computation — a region (A region is nesting, not a flat CFG) taking two scalars and yielding one — rather than an enum of built-in reductions. Any associative operation can therefore be expressed, including ones the dialect never enumerated.
The form above is sugar for the common case; the general form spells the region out with a stablehlo.return. dimensions lists the dims removed from the operand shape.
The init value is not decoration — it is the identity of the reducer, and it is also what a zero-sized reduction returns. Getting it wrong (0 for a max, say) produces a reduction that is right on non-empty input and silently wrong at the edge.
HLO's reduce is the same design with to_apply naming the computation (reduce removes the dims it lists).

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Backlinks
Mosaic

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The TPU kernel compiler Pallas lowers to — an MLIR pipeline over a tpu dialect, sitting where Triton sits on GPU. A Pallas TPU kernel becomes a serialised Mosaic module inside a @tpu_custom_call attribute (A Pallas kernel is an opaque custom call), which XLA then treats as a black box (A custom call is a black box XLA cannot fuse across).

What makes a Mosaic dump feel unlike a GPU one is that there are no threads in it (Mosaic is explicit memory spaces and explicit copies). A GPU IR is a thread and warp hierarchy in which data movement is implicit in which thread touches what. Mosaic is the opposite: explicit memory spaces on every memref (A memref names storage, a tensor is a value) — hbm, VMEM, smem — explicit DMA-style copies between them, semaphores for synchronisation, and vector ops on hardware tile shapes, typically 8 \times 128 for f32 (Vectors are register-level, tensors are abstract).

That is the same shift Pallas asks of you at the source level, and the reason a TPU kernel is written as a pipeline of asynchronous copies rather than as an indexing scheme: the machine has no thread-level parallelism to hide a bad access pattern behind, so the copies have to be scheduled rather than merely correct.

fr:title.text: A custom call is a black box XLA cannot fuse across

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A custom call is a black box XLA cannot fuse across

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read custom-call(%a, %b), custom_call_target="tpu_custom_call", operand_layout_constraints={...}, backend_config="...", api_version=API_VERSION_STATUS_RETURNING

html:div.html:details:
Answer The escape hatch to code XLA does not generate: library kernels (cuBLAS, cuDNN), Pallas and Mosaic or Triton kernels (A Pallas kernel is an opaque custom call), host callbacks.
custom_call_target selects the registered handler by name.
backend_config carries the opaque payload — a serialised Mosaic module, a tuning configuration, an algorithm choice.
operand_layout_constraints pins the layouts the handler requires (The layout is minor-to-major).
Everything expensive about a custom call follows from XLA not being able to see inside it. It cannot fuse across the boundary, so the operands are materialised to High bandwidth memory and the results read back; it must assume the declared effects, so it cannot reorder freely; and the pinned layouts can force copy ops on both sides (bitcast is free, copy is not).
A hand-written kernel has to beat all of that, not just the kernel XLA would have emitted.

The kernel body is not in this IR. It is serialised inside backend_config — a Mosaic module, or Triton IR (The prefix says which side of layout assignment) — and XLA treats the whole thing as a black box with declared operands, results, and effects.
That is the trade you accept when you write a kernel by hand: you get control of the inner loop, and you give up every cross-op optimisation at the boundary, because the compiler cannot fuse across something it cannot see (A custom call is a black box XLA cannot fuse across).

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Triton

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A Python-embedded DSL for GPU kernels in which you write block-level code — load a tile, do arithmetic on it, store it — and the compiler decides how the tile maps onto threads [tilletTritonIntermediateLanguage2019]. That is the trade against CUDA: you give up control of the thread indexing that memory coalescing depends on, and in exchange you stop writing it.

The compiler is built on MLIR, with two custom dialects, and the boundary between them is the single most useful thing to know when a kernel is slow (The prefix says which side of layout assignment). ttir (tt. ops) is the target-independent tensor level — roughly what you wrote. ttgir (ttg. ops) is after layout assignment, where every tensor carries an encoding saying which lane holds which element (An encoding tiles the block across threads and warps).

So a Triton performance problem is one of two things, and the dialect prefix tells you which. At the tt. level it is your algorithm — the tiling, the loop structure, the arithmetic. At the ttg. level it is the compiler's distribution of it, and the usual culprit is a ttg.convert_layout that round-trips a tensor through shared memory inside a loop (A convert_layout round-trips through shared memory). The second kind is invisible in your source and obvious in the IR, which is the argument for reading the IR.

From XLA's side a Triton kernel is an opaque @triton_kernel_call custom call (XLA custom call, A custom call is a black box XLA cannot fuse across), so nothing fuses across it — the same bargain Pallas makes on TPU.

fr:title.text: The prefix says which side of layout assignment

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The prefix says which side of layout assignment

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What do the tt. and ttg. (triton_gpu) prefixes separate in Triton IR?

html:div.html:details:
Answer tt. is the target-independent tensor level: tt.load, tt.store, tt.dot, tt.make_range, and pointer arithmetic on !tt.ptr<f32> over block shapes. This is roughly what you wrote.
ttg. is after layout assignment: the same tensors now carry an encoding attribute saying how their elements are distributed across warps, lanes, and registers (An encoding tiles the block across threads and warps), plus ops like ttg.convert_layout (A convert_layout round-trips through shared memory) and shared-memory allocation (Shared memory (GPU)).
So the prefix tells you which side of layout assignment you are on, and that is the division that matters when a Triton kernel is slow: a problem at the tt. level is your algorithm, and a problem that only appears at ttg. is the compiler's distribution of it. Same use of the dialect prefix as a marker of pipeline stage as chlo / stablehlo / mhlo (chlo desugars, stablehlo is stable, mhlo is internal).

fr:title.text: An encoding tiles the block across threads and warps

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: An encoding tiles the block across threads and warps

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read tensor<128x64xf16, #blocked> where #blocked = #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread=[1,4], threadsPerWarp=[8,4], warpsPerCTA=[4,1], order=[1,0]}>

html:div.html:details:
Answer The encoding says how the logical 128 \times 64 tile is distributed:
sizePerThread — elements each thread holds per dimension; the minor-dimension entry is the vectorisation width.
threadsPerWarp — how the 32 lanes of a Warp (GPU) are arranged in two dimensions.
warpsPerCTA — how warps tile the block.
order — minor-to-major, so which dimension is contiguous per thread (The layout is minor-to-major).
Multiply the three lists out and you get the tile one CTA covers in one pass: 1 \times 8 \times 4 = 32 rows and 4 \times 4 \times 1 = 16 columns here, so the 128 \times 64 shape takes 4 \times 4 repeats. That arithmetic is the whole content of the attribute, and it is how you check by hand whether loads coalesce.

fr:title.text: A convert_layout round-trips through shared memory

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A convert_layout round-trips through shared memory

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Why is ttg.convert_layout the op to look for in a slow Triton kernel?

html:div.html:details:
Answer It re-distributes a tensor from one encoding to another (An encoding tiles the block across threads and warps) — typically #blocked to a #ttg.dot_op or #mma operand layout, because the tensor core wants its operands arranged differently from the way the loads produced them.
Unless the conversion happens to be a pure register permutation, it round-trips through shared memory and inserts barriers. That is a store, a sync across the block, and a load — for data that never changed value.
One unnecessary convert_layout inside a loop body is a classic Triton performance bug, and it is visible in the IR long before it is visible in a profile. The layout-propagation passes exist to hoist these out of loops or eliminate them, so one that survives in the body is worth understanding rather than accepting.

fr:title.text: A custom call is a black box XLA cannot fuse across

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A custom call is a black box XLA cannot fuse across

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read custom-call(%a, %b), custom_call_target="tpu_custom_call", operand_layout_constraints={...}, backend_config="...", api_version=API_VERSION_STATUS_RETURNING

html:div.html:details:
Answer The escape hatch to code XLA does not generate: library kernels (cuBLAS, cuDNN), Pallas and Mosaic or Triton kernels (A Pallas kernel is an opaque custom call), host callbacks.
custom_call_target selects the registered handler by name.
backend_config carries the opaque payload — a serialised Mosaic module, a tuning configuration, an algorithm choice.
operand_layout_constraints pins the layouts the handler requires (The layout is minor-to-major).
Everything expensive about a custom call follows from XLA not being able to see inside it. It cannot fuse across the boundary, so the operands are materialised to High bandwidth memory and the results read back; it must assume the declared effects, so it cannot reorder freely; and the pinned layouts can force copy ops on both sides (bitcast is free, copy is not).
A hand-written kernel has to beat all of that, not just the kernel XLA would have emitted.

fr:title.text: Why Custom Kernels?

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Why Custom Kernels?

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Example. In attention kernel, we perform QK^T in VMEM then copy back to HBM, then copy back to VMEM and do the softmax. Instead we want to fuse this into one kernel.

html:figure.html:figcaption: Summary of XLA fusions for attention kernel.

html:ul.html:li: Logit & Max fusion:
34.45% flop utilization
Use MXU to get over 350TFLOP/s.
18.74% HBM bandwidth utilization.
3.55% On-chip read utilization
Softmax denom:
0.32% flop utilization.
0.0% HBM bandwidth utilization.
Keeps 1024x1024 logit matrix resident in VMEM.
22.61% On-chip read utilization
Uses VPU to compute softmax which consumes data from VMEM at 6.6 TB/s.
Attention output:
35.82% flop utilization.
19.49% HBM bandwidth utilization.
7.39% On-chip read utilization.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: HBM Bottleneck. The default XLA attention does not fuse the softmax with the logit computation, requiring the entire logit matrix to be written back to HBM.
Vector Unit Limitations. MXU can be left idle while VPU is performing copmlex exponential and sum operations.
VMEM Residency and Loop Control. Pallas allows you to control data movement, so that we can explicitly enforce online softmax rather than writing back to HBM.
Temporal Control via LLO. Pallas also allows control over the temporal flow, preventing the compiler from reordering your manual optimizations.

fr:title.text: Pallas Fundamentals

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Pallas Fundamentals

html:ul.html:li: Inside the kernel, data has already been moved from HBM to VMEM.
If data exceeds VMEM, we need to tile with BlockSpec.
Also need to pipeline i.e. while doing computation on a given block, we need to be moving the next block from HBM to VMEM.
By default, pipelining is done for you, but there are other APIs to control this(?)
For-Loop scheduler.
Asynchronous overlap.
Buffer reuse. Uses same VMEM buffer across iterations.
Macro-tiling: this is done by Pallas / user. You define the larger software blocks i.e. 1024x1024 to hide latency DMA transfers. Pallas manages pipeling.
Micro-tiling: this is done by compiler / hardware. Translates larger block into hardware native VREG 8x128.
VLOAD: fetching inputs for chunk (8x128)(N + 1)th from VMEM and move to VRegs
VALU: Perform elementwise operations for current (Nth) chunk
VSTORE: write completed result for previous (N - 1)th chunk from VRegs back to VMEM.

fr:title.text: Flash Attention

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Flash Attention

html:ul.html:li: Each block does a local softmax calculation.
Tracks a shared maximum and adjusts results.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Can Now fuse score calculation, softmax, and value aggregation into single pass.
No longer need to store NxN attention matrix in HBM.
Can break Q, K, V into small blocks that fit in VMEM.
Kernel available here.

html:ul.html:li: Dynamic scaling (\alpha ): Computes e^{m_{prev} - m_{next}} to track change in maximum logit across blocks for numerical stability.
Re-scale accumulation: Multiplies by \alpha to the previously accumulated sums before adding current block output to accurately rescale all past results.
Additive updates: partial results (current softmax and outputs) are added to running totals via fast multiply and addition ops.
Delayed normalization: only divide by normalization once at the very end of the loop because division is slow.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Block-size tuning. to maximize compute-to-load ratio need biggest block sizes that fit into VMEM.

fr:title.text: Splash Attention

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Splash Attention

fr:mainmatter.html:p: With certain masks (i.e. causal) can skip alot of computation for parts of the attention matrix that are being masked out.

html:ul.html:li: Finer blocks -> can skip more but then have poorer utilization.
Sparsity pruning: Divide mask into blocks and discard all inactive blocks (all zeros).
Data compression: see how many unique mask patterns are needed to describe the remaining active blocks.
Execution map and pre-fetching: (active_rows, mask_next) generated to map the computation order and tell the MXU which mask pattern to prefetch for zero-latency application.
Block filtering (block_mask): categorizes QK blocks as zero, non-zero, partial.
Coordinate mapping (active_ros/cols): provides the hardware with (Q, KV) grid indices, ensuring efficient loading of active blocks from HBM.
Mask pipelining (mask_next): tells the hardware which mask pattern to prefetch.
SMEM-resident metadata: computed once per mask and stored in SMEM. Enable high-speed access to sparse execution map without need to re-transfer from HBM.
Grid definition: defined by (num_q_heads, grid_size). Grid size is set dynamically using the sparese meta data fwd_mask_info.num_active_blocks[0].
SMEM Inputs: num_scalar_prefetch instructs hardware to prefetch critical scalar/metadata inputs into SMEM before thread begins computing.
VMEM Inputs: (Q, K, V) that must be moved from HBM to VMEM for kernel to execute.
